concepts.title: Conic Sections as Plane-Cone Intersections
concepts.definition: Slice a double-napped right circular cone with a flat plane and the cut edge traces one of the classic curves -- circle, ellipse, parabola or hyperbola depending on the tilt of the slice; degenerate slices give a point, a straight line or a crossing pair of lines. These curves are called conic sections or conics.
concepts.key_idea: One cone, one plane, four families of curves -- the tilt of the slice alone decides which conic appears.
concepts.textbook_ref: kemh110.txt lines 40-100 (sections 10.2, 10.2.1, 10.2.2; sections of a cone, degenerated conic sections, Apollonius naming)

solution_steps.action: set up the cone and plane
solution_steps.explain: A double-napped right circular cone meets a moving plane; the intersection curve is the conic.
A plane parallel to the generator gives a parabola; a smaller tilt gives an ellipse (a circle when it is horizontal); a steeper cut through both nappes gives a hyperbola.
A plane through the vertex yields a point, a single line or two intersecting lines -- the degenerate conics.

concepts.title: Circle: Centre and Radius from the General Equation
concepts.definition: A circle is the set of points at one fixed distance (the radius) from a fixed centre. Written as x^2 + y^2 + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0, the circle hides its centre at (-g, -f) and its radius squared equals g^2 + f^2 - c, which must stay positive for a real circle.
concepts.key_idea: Complete two squares in your head: the coefficients of x and y give the centre, and the leftover constant fixes the radius.
concepts.textbook_ref: kemh110.txt lines 91-180 (section 10.3 circle, standard equation, general form x^2 + y^2 + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0)
question_patterns: find the centre and radius of the circle with the given equation

write the equation of the circle with given centre passing through a given point
determine whether the given point lies inside or outside the circle

solution_steps.explain: Matching 2gx + 2fy against the equation gives g and f directly as half the x and y coefficients.
The radius is the square root of g squared plus f squared minus c.

concepts.title: Parabola: Focus, Directrix and Standard Equations
concepts.definition: A parabola collects the points that stay equally far from a fixed point (the focus) and a fixed line (the directrix). Placed with vertex at the origin, the four standard equations are y^2 = 4ax (opens right), y^2 = -4ax (left), x^2 = 4ay (up) and x^2 = -4ay (down), with the axis of symmetry deciding the direction.
concepts.key_idea: Equal distances to focus and directrix -- the one defining balance that shapes every parabola.
concepts.textbook_ref: kemh110.txt lines 215-345 (section 10.4 and 10.4.1, focus, directrix, axis, vertex, four standard equations of parabola)

solution_steps.explain: Every point of the parabola satisfies distance to focus = perpendicular distance to directrix.
A y-squared term with x on the other side means the parabola opens along the x-axis; x-squared opens along the y-axis.
Comparing with y^2 = 4ax puts the focus at (a, 0) and the directrix at x = -a; the sign of a fixes the opening direction.

concepts.title: Latus Rectum of a Parabola
concepts.definition: The chord of a parabola that runs through the focus parallel to the directrix is its latus rectum; for the standard parabola with focal distance a it stretches to length 4a, and it is the widest double-width chord the curve cuts at the focus height.
concepts.key_idea: Endpoints of the latus rectum sit at (a, plus/minus 2a) -- four times the focal distance end to end.
concepts.textbook_ref: kemh110.txt lines 346-380 (section 10.4.2 latus rectum of a parabola, endpoints (a, 2a) and (a, -2a))

solution_steps.explain: In y^2 = 4ax the focal distance is the coefficient a, obtained by dividing the y-squared coefficient by 4.
The chord across the focus measures 4a from end to end.

concepts.title: Ellipse: Standard Equation, Foci and Axes
concepts.definition: An ellipse is the path of points whose distances from two fixed foci add to one constant. In standard position its equation reads x^2/a^2 + y^2/b^2 = 1 with a the semi-major and b the semi-minor axis, foci on the major axis at plus or minus c where c^2 = a^2 - b^2.
concepts.key_idea: Constant sum of distances to two foci -- and the semi-minor axis is the height at the ellipse's centre width.
concepts.textbook_ref: kemh110.txt lines 381-470 and 500-560 (section 10.5, 10.5.1 relationship between semi-major and semi-minor axis, foci)

solution_steps.explain: For every point on the ellipse the two focal distances add to the same total 2a.

solution_steps.action: identify the axes from the equation
solution_steps.explain: The larger denominator sits under the axis that carries the foci -- that is the major axis.
The focal half-distance satisfies c^2 = a^2 - b^2, the same Pythagorean link used for the eccentricity.

concepts.title: Eccentricity of an Ellipse
concepts.definition: Eccentricity grades how stretched an ellipse is: the ratio of the focal half-distance to the semi-major axis, always a number between 0 and 1. At e = 0 the foci merge and the ellipse is a circle; as e climbs toward 1 the ellipse flattens.
concepts.key_idea: e = c/a sits strictly between 0 and 1 -- zero means circle, near one means long and thin.
concepts.textbook_ref: kemh110.txt lines 560-585 (section 10.5.2 eccentricity of an ellipse, e = c/a less than 1)

solution_steps.explain: Pythagoras on the semi-axes gives c = sqrt(a^2 - b^2).
e = c / a lands between 0 and 1 because b stays positive.

concepts.title: Latus Rectum of an Ellipse
concepts.definition: The latus rectum of an ellipse is the chord through a focus at right angles to the major axis; its length is 2b^2/a, twice the square of the semi-minor axis divided by the semi-major axis.
concepts.key_idea: Plug x = c into the ellipse equation: the y-extent there is b^2/a on each side, doubling to the chord length.
concepts.textbook_ref: kemh110.txt lines 586-610 (section 10.5.4 latus rectum of an ellipse, length 2b^2/a)

solution_steps.explain: The half-chord at the focus is b^2/a, so b^2 is needed first.
Multiplying by 2 and dividing by the semi-major axis gives the full chord.

concepts.title: Hyperbola: Standard Equation, Axes and Eccentricity
concepts.definition: A hyperbola is the set of points for which the difference of distances to two fixed foci stays constant. Its standard equation is x^2/a^2 - y^2/b^2 = 1 with a transverse axis of length 2a and a conjugate axis of length 2b; here the focal half-distance obeys c^2 = a^2 + b^2, so the eccentricity c/a always exceeds 1.
concepts.key_idea: Same shape of equation as the ellipse but a minus sign -- and that flips the focal relation from a^2 - b^2 to a^2 + b^2, pushing e past 1.
concepts.textbook_ref: kemh110.txt lines 611-700 (sections 10.6, 10.6.1 eccentricity, 10.6.2 standard equation of hyperbola, 10.6.3 latus rectum)
